newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-NAB sharpens focus on Asian markets.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-NAB sharpens focus on Asian markets.

text.p: Australia's most profitable bank, National Australia Bank Ltd (NAB), said on Thursday it was continuing to push into the burgeoning Asian banking sector which it considers a key part of the bank's global network.

"Our strategy is to concentrate our efforts on specific areas and build our operations there through a mix of organic growth, alliances and integration into the group's emerging global network," chairman William Irvine said.
Irvine told the bank's annual meeting that NAB had identified a number of business segments in the Asian region that fit into the group's global aspirations.
"In the area of wholesale banking, for example, we believe there is scope for a global approach to corporate banking, project and structured finance, treasury and capital markets," he said.

The bank, which already has treasury operations in Tokyo, Hong Kong and Singapore, has turned to Asian markets for growth at a time when margins in its home market of Australia are under pressure due to intensifying competition.
"Our international spread of assets places us in a far stronger position to weather the slowdown in local activity than many other Australian-based companies," Irvine said.
NAB's managing director, Don Argus, said the bank was scrutinising several alliance options in the Asian region, but he would not give specific details.
"We've looked at a few (alliances) with banks, other institutions ... It takes time to pull these things off," Argus told reporters after the annual meeting.
He said Asian countries offered a wealth of both margin and fee-based income opportunites.
Thursday's meeting coincided with the group's announcement of stronger-than-expected first quarter results.
NAB's net profit for the three months to December 31 jumped 13.5 percent to A$582 million.
Lower costs and diminishing bad debts helped underpin the result as did improved earnings from its other offshore operations in Britain, the United States and New Zealand.
